articles.title: A Connecticut man paid $35 for a bowl at a yard sale in 2020; experts revealed it was a rare 15th-century Chinese treasure and it sold for $721,800
articles.summary: A Connecticut man paid $35 for a small blue-and-white porcelain bowl at a yard sale near New Haven in 2020, unaware that he had stumbled upon an
articles.body: A Connecticut man paid $35 for a small blue-and-white porcelain bowl at a yard sale near New Haven in 2020, unaware that he had stumbled upon an exceptionally rare Chinese imperial-era artefact. The unnamed antiques enthusiast suspected the bowl might be special and later sent photographs to Sotheby's for an evaluation. Specialists identified it as a Ming dynasty bowl dating to the early 15th century, during the reign of the Yongle Emperor. Only seven comparable bowls were known to exist, including the Connecticut discovery. Sotheby's initially estimated that it could sell for $300,000 to $500,000. When the bowl went under the hammer in New York on March 17, 2021, it attracted 15 bids and eventually sold for $721,800, including fees.A $35 find at a Connecticut yard saleThe discovery began at a yard sale in the New Haven area in 2020. The buyer, whose identity was not disclosed, was an antiques enthusiast browsing the items when he noticed the small porcelain bowl.Unlike someone who simply stumbled across an object by chance, the buyer apparently had enough knowledge to suspect that the bowl could be valuable. He paid the $35 asking price without haggling and took it home. He later contacted Sotheby's and sent photographs of the piece, asking the auction house to assess it.The decision to seek an expert opinion proved crucial. Sotheby's receives photographs and inquiries about potentially valuable objects regularly, but specialists Angela McAteer, head of the auction house's Chinese works of art department, and specialist Hang Yin recognised something unusual in the bowl. When they examined it in person, they determined that its shape, glaze, cobalt-blue decoration and other characteristics were consistent with early 15th-century Chinese porcelain.Experts identify a Ming dynasty treasureSotheby's identified the object as an exceptional blue-and-white floral bowl from the Ming dynasty's Yongle period. The Yongle Emperor ruled from 1403 to 1424, placing the bowl's production in the early 15th century.The bowl measures approximately 6¼ inches, or 16 centimetres, in diameter. Its shape resembles a lotus bud or what is sometimes described as a chicken-heart form. The interior contains a central medallion and intricate floral and geometric decoration, while the exterior features four different flowers: lotus, peony, chrysanthemum and pomegranate.Sotheby's described the piece as a quintessential example of Yongle-period porcelain made for the imperial court. During the Yongle reign, the imperial kilns at Jingdezhen produced sophisticated blue-and-white porcelain, and the bowl reflects the distinctive craftsmanship and decorative style associated with that period.Only seven comparable bowls were knownThe bowl's age was only part of what made it remarkable. Its rarity was even more significant.Sotheby's specialists said that only six other comparable bowls were known to exist, making seven including the Connecticut example. Most were held by major museums and institutions rather than private American collections.Known examples included bowls in collections associated with the National Palace Museum in Taipei, museums in London and the National Museum of Iran in Tehran. Sotheby's said there were no other examples of the type in US museums at the time.The fact that such a scarce imperial-era object had appeared at an ordinary Connecticut yard sale made its discovery particularly striking. How the bowl reached the sale was not known. Sotheby's suggested that it may have passed through generations of a family that did not realise how unusual it was.Sotheby's estimates the bowl at up to $500,000After authentication, Sotheby's prepared the bowl for its Important Chinese Art auction in New York. The auction house placed a presale estimate of $300,000 to $500,000.That estimate represented an extraordinary jump from the $35 paid at the yard sale. At the upper estimate of $500,000, the bowl would already have been worth more than 14,000 times its purchase price.The auction listing provided extensive details about the bowl's construction and decoration. Sotheby's described its rich cobalt-blue painting, delicate floral motifs and distinctive shape, all of which helped specialists establish its relationship to Yongle-period imperial porcelain.Fifteen bids push the price beyond expectationsThe bowl was offered at Sotheby's New York on March 17, 2021, as part of the auction house's Important Chinese Art sale during Asia Week.Bidding quickly moved beyond the lower end of the estimate. Contemporary reports said the auction attracted 15 bids, beginning at $200,000 from an online bidder. The competition eventually pushed the hammer price to $580,000.After Sotheby's fees were added, the official price realised was $721,800. Four bidders were reported to have competed for the bowl during the auction.The final price substantially exceeded Sotheby's $500,000 upper estimate. Compared with the original $35 purchase, the $721,800 result represented more than 20,000 times what the buyer had paid.A bowl made for the Yongle courtThe Yongle period was an important stage in the development of Chinese blue-and-white porcelain. The imperial court encouraged new styles and high-quality production at the Jingdezhen kilns in present-day Jiangxi province.The Connecticut bowl reflects that tradition through its carefully painted floral decoration. The outside alternates lotus, peony, chrysanthemum and pomegranate blossoms with other decorative emblems, while the interior contains additional geometric and floral designs.Its small size also belies the complexity of its decoration. Despite measuring only about 16 centimetres across, the bowl contains multiple layers of painted motifs and carefully executed patterns.From an ordinary yard sale to a major auctionThe buyer had paid the $35 asking price after spotting the bowl at a yard sale. Rather than leaving it as an unidentified piece of pottery, he sought professional advice and contacted Sotheby's. That decision led specialists to identify a rare Ming dynasty object that had survived for more than six centuries.The bowl's final auction price also showed the importance of rarity, craftsmanship and imperial provenance in the market for Chinese ceramics. Its appearance at a New Haven-area yard sale remains unexplained, but its subsequent examination established that the seemingly modest purchase was an exceptionally rare example of Yongle-period porcelain.On March 17, 2021, the $35 yard-sale purchase completed its extraordinary transformation when it sold at Sotheby's for $721,800 including fees.You use AI every day. articles.title: U.S. can deport the leader of Wisconsin’s largest mosque on national security grounds, judge rules
articles.summary: The U.S. can deport Salah Sarsour, the leader of Wisconsin’s largest mosque, on the grounds that he is a threat to national security, an immigration judge ruled Wednesday.
articles.body: CHICAGO — The U.S. can deport the leader of Wisconsin’s largest mosque on the grounds that he is a threat to national security, an immigration judge ruled Wednesday. Salah Sarsour was detained in Milwaukee in March by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers. A federal judge ordered Sarsour’s release in June, saying he raised a “substantial” claim that the Trump administration was targeting him for speaking out against Israel and advocating for Palestinian rights. Sarsour called the ruling “deeply disappointing,” but said he intends to appeal. “I will continue fighting to defend the right to free speech and to stay in the country I have called home for more than three decades,” Sarsour said in a statement. Government attorneys say Sarsour’s decades-old convictions in Israel make him a threat to national security and accuse him of lying on his green card application and falsely claiming citizenship to vote. Judge Jayme Salinardi, with the Chicago Immigration Court, found him removable on foreign policy grounds but tossed out the government’s claim that Sarsour lied to immigration authorities. “All illegal aliens receive due process,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement. “If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them. Period.” Sarsour says his life will be at risk if he is deported to the West Bank Sarsour, who was born in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, was imprisoned in Israel in 1988 after being convicted of throwing stones at Israeli military personnel. DHS has said he was also convicted of throwing a Molotov cocktail. His defense team says he was accused of that but not convicted. In 1995, he was convicted of attempting to possess weapons. Sarsour denies committing those crimes and his attorneys say he was tortured and coerced into confessing in both instances. Sarsour, the president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee, does not have a criminal record in the U.S., where he has lived since 1993. His attorneys say the U.S. government has known about Sarsour’s convictions in Israel since he arrived. Deportation to the West Bank “means the end of my life,” Sarsour told The Associated Press on Tuesday. One of his attorneys, Patrick Taurel, said Sarsour’s treatment by Israeli authorities is “probably a good indicator of what awaits him” if he is deported. At a status hearing Wednesday, Taurel pressed the judge to specify that Sarsour can only be deported to Israel or the Palestinian territories. Jordan, a country to which Sarsour has no connection, is listed as a possible destination on the order of removal. Sarsour was instructed by immigration officers to list Jordan as his home country on an immigration form because his preferred entry — “Palestine” — is not a fully independent, unified state. But he “has no right to reside in Jordan,” Taurel said. Salinardi declined, saying that can be addressed on appeal. If sent to Jordan, Sarsour “would just be immediately handed off to Israel,” Taurel said during a news conference Wednesday. Attorney says Sarsour will fight deportation Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a memo in June 2025 invoking a rarely used immigration provision saying Sarsour could be deported on the same grounds as Mahmoud Khalil and Mohsen Mahdawi, both advocates for Palestinian rights whom the Trump administration has tried to expel, according to court documents. DHS said in its statement that Rubio “has reasonable grounds to believe Sarsour’s presence would have adverse foreign policy consequences for the U.S., and he has engaged in terrorist activity or supported a terrorist organization.” Salinardi found Rubio’s letter singling out Sarsour as a foreign policy risk was “presumptive and sufficient evidence” that the government can remove him, Taurel said Wednesday, reading from the judge’s decision. The judge gave “extreme deference” to Rubio and to Israel, which has “collaborated” with DHS in the effort to deport Sarsour, the attorney said. Taurel has said Sarsour will need to demonstrate that he could be tortured again if he were deported, calling it a “very high bar” that he believes his team “can meet in this case.” A notice of appeal is due within 30 days, and Sarsour has 60 days to file an application for relief. The government cannot deport Sarsour until he has exhausted all available legal avenues. Salinardi, who did not schedule a new hearing, announced he is retiring and that Judge Craig Defoe will oversee the case going forward. Sarsour says he was tortured and coerced into confessions Jawad Boulos, who represented Sarsour when he was convicted in Israel, testified in August that Sarsour was coerced into confessing and that he wasn’t convicted of any charge tying him to a terrorist organization. He said Sarsour was tortured by Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency. The Department of Homeland Security challenged Boulos about the torture allegations, questioning how he could know it was true. Sarsour’s defense team has repeatedly asked why the government waited until this year to detain him, saying it has known of his imprisonment in Israel for decades. Experts on forced confessions and the treatment of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli prisons also testified in Sarsour’s defense. Israeli military courts have faced repeated scrutiny over allegations of limited due process and the high conviction rate of Palestinians. Israel rejects the claims. In June, U.S. District Judge James Patrick Hanlon ordered Sarsour released from ICE custody saying he could have a case arguing the U.S. government detained him in retaliation for protected speech. Further, Hanlon said, government attorneys had not explained why Sarsour was suddenly considered a threat after decades as a lawful permanent resident. The Trump administration has appealed Hanlon’s ruling. Sarsour, who has Type 2 diabetes, lost more than 30 pounds (14 kilograms) while detained by ICE, and his blood sugar levels were checked only once a month, putting him at risk of organ failure or death, his attorneys said. An investigation by KFF Health News and The Associated Press found that hundreds of detainees in at least 33 states have filed federal lawsuits with similar allegations of medical neglect.

articles.title: Actor Luke Evans 'selfishly' found role in ITV drama The Party
articles.summary: Actor Luke Evans came up with the idea to adapt the acclaimed novel by Elizabeth Day into a TV drama.
articles.body:
Hollywood actor Luke Evans has said he "selfishly" found himself a leading role in a new TV drama, The Party.

The Pontypool-born actor, who is also an executive producer of the five-part series, came up with the idea to adapt the acclaimed novel by Elizabeth Day into a drama for the screen.

After reading the book, Evans said he thought to himself: "This is just so fun. It's my kind of story. I love the narrative. I love the characters. Selfishly, there was also a great leading role that I could play."

Evans will star as Martin Gilmour, a journalist shaped by his lifelong friendship with a wealthy and charismatic politician played by Aberystwyth-born Tom Cullen.

Evans brought the idea to World Productions, who he previously worked with on The Pembrokeshire Murders , and said: "I think we should do this together."

The actor said it did not take much to convince them, adding: "It was a no-brainer really."

The thriller moves between the birthday party of Cullen's character, Ben Fitzmaurice, and a police investigation that follows.

Evans previously said he drew on his own experiences to play the character , who is described as a "calculated and buttoned-up man".

"I think that's probably why I resonated with the story when I read the book," Evans said.

Evans said coming from a "very working-class background" helped him understand his character's choices.

"Even though it probably wouldn't have been my choice of journey, I understood him.

"I got the fact that, through a strange route, this man got what he wanted and succeeded. He came from nothing, but was very clever, almost chameleon-like, in how he could adapt and observe and blend in, and I just thought it was very interesting," he said.

Evans said Gilmour is treated like "an outsider by almost everybody" in the drama which starts on Sunday on ITV.

"This kid gets an opportunity to go to an Eton-style school. But he sticks out like a sore thumb and is treated as an outsider by almost everybody.

"I have always felt like an outsider myself," Evans said, recalling when he first began working in the film industry.

"When I first became a film actor, I didn't feel like I belonged.

"I didn't feel accepted in the way I saw other people of my age and peer group being accepted. So Martin resonated a lot with me."

"I also admired him," Evans added, because despite the obstacles he faced, as "it didn't stop him from keeping going".

"He was a fighter. He was able to manoeuvre himself into the right places, so the opportunities arose. It's a very relatable story."

Evans said portraying Gilmour also reminded him of when he started musical theatre college in London.

"I was the only Welsh person there. I felt like my accent stood out among all these English accents," he said.

"I hadn't been brought up with the idea that I would go to musical theatre college. I was a Jehovah's Witness," which Evans previously said led him to hide his sexuality .

"I was brought up thinking I was going to become a window cleaner, and knock doors... So I related to that side of Martin as well.

"He had to change his story and needed to be seen around certain people for him to progress. I just thought it was really brave of him," Evans said.

"Martin saw the landed gentry with their long drives and their big gates and their crumbling country piles, all expecting their children to inherit and do something grand and remarkable with their lives. But nothing was really expected of Martin.

"Martin just expected things of himself."

articles.title: After Utah removed invasive brown trout from a mountain stream for 4 years, native Bonneville cutthroat trout recovered to near-carrying capacity within 6 years
articles.summary: A groundbreaking study reveals how Utah's Right Hand Fork stream successfully restored populations of native Bonneville cutthroat trout after eliminating invasive brown trout, demonstrating rapid ecosystem recovery and the importance of habitat management.
articles.body: Removing an established fish population from a mountain stream is not a simple task. Even after the unwanted fish are gone, there is no guarantee that native species will return in large numbers. In a tributary of Utah's Logan River, however, researchers found that native Bonneville cutthroat trout could recover surprisingly quickly after non-native brown trout were removed.According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), the long-running experiment took place in Right Hand Fork, a tributary where non-native brown trout had become established alongside the native Bonneville cutthroat trout. Researchers had monitored the fish community for a decade before beginning the removal programme. The four-year effort included two years of mechanical removal followed by two years of chemical treatment. After the brown trout were eradicated, the researchers introduced relatively small numbers of cutthroat trout eggs and young fish. Within six years of the eradication, the native population had recovered to close to the stream's estimated carrying capacity.Removing the fish that had taken overAccording to Conservation Science and Practice, the Right Hand Fork is part of the Logan River watershed in northern Utah and provides habitat for Bonneville cutthroat trout. Brown trout had become established in the tributary by the late 1990s, and before the restoration work, the stream was dominated by the non-native species rather than supporting a resident population of cutthroat trout. Researchers identified competition from brown trout as one of the pressures affecting native cutthroat trout in the wider Logan River system. The researchers first spent 10 years collecting information on the stream's fish populations. This gave them a baseline against which they could measure what happened after the brown trout were removed.The first step involved the use of mechanical removal techniques such as electro-fishing. After this came the second stage, which involved two years of chemical application, aiming at eliminating all the brown trout. This four-year process was not simply one of removing all the fish once and then letting the stream take care of itself. It took repeated efforts since brown trout would live or come back to a part of a stream system. Past experience in the Logan River had proved how hard it was to get rid of brown trout. Through two years of mechanical removal, 15,000 brown trout were removed from 5.6 kilometers of Right Hand Fork.Native trout get another chanceAfter the removal of brown trout from the ecosystem, however, the scientists did not leave the recovery process to chance. They introduced a small number of eggs and young fish of cutthroat trout into the ecosystem. In this way, the experiment evaluated the influence of both factors – elimination of the competitor and the introduction of a new source population for the native fish. Results came fast. Scientists calculated the growth rate and the carrying capacity of the population based on monitoring results during several years. After six years of eradication and seeding of brown trout population reached the carrying capacity of the stream. At least four age classes existed, including adult fish suitable for anglers.The recovery was also consistent with earlier research showing that brown trout can affect the performance of native Bonneville cutthroat trout. A field experiment published in Transactions of the American Fisheries Society examined brown trout's effects on native cutthroat trout at both individual and population levels, providing evidence that interactions between the two species can influence the native fish population. The result was therefore not simply a case of fish numbers rising after a stocking exercise. The restoration removed a competing non-native population and then allowed the native fish to establish themselves in habitat that had previously been occupied by brown trout.What the recovery tells researchersThe modelling of the cutthroat population by the researchers gave an optimistic long-term outlook. This is because the model showed that there was a 95% chance that the cutthroat trout population would have attained at least 90% of its carrying capacity after 10 years of brown trout eradication. This does not mean all the streams will show a similar trend. The study location had healthy habitat, and the researchers stated that removal of invader species could be influenced by the size and status of the ecosystem, among other factors.However, they also noted that such small tributaries as the Right Hand Fork were constrained by size. Any larger benefits might result from their ability to serve as source populations that enable native trout to thrive in the downstream reaches of a river system. The research provided an informative illustration of how the native fish might fare in conditions when they have the opportunity for restoration. Four years of brown trout elimination and six years of monitoring resulted in the population of Bonneville cutthroat trout being on par with the maximum capacity of the stream to support them. The restoration did not take several decades but was fast.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Tropical Pacific moisture drenches central U.S. as another Pacific hurricane forms
articles.summary: Tropical weather that surged onshore from the Pacific soaked more of the U.S. while forecasters announced yet another hurricane Rachel off the coast of Mexico.
articles.body: Tropical weather that surged onshore from the Pacific soaked more of the U.S. on Wednesday while forecasters announced yet another hurricane off the coast of Mexico. The new hurricane, Rachel, is expected to develop rapidly and could become a major one with sustained winds topping 111 mph (178 kph). The storm was far offshore, however, and posed no threat to land. Parts of New Mexico, meanwhile, looked less and less like the months of drought that dried up reservoirs and caused hungry bears to roam into neighborhoods in search of food. Wednesday marks the end of the second wettest month ever in Albuquerque, with National Weather Service records dating back to the 1800s. Flood warnings in the southwestern state remained in effect, despite the storm slowing. “There’s a lot of standing water in the fields and near some homes,” National Weather Service meteorologist Greg Lundeen said of one area where water overtopped a minor dam. Floodwaters threatened the state’s famous chile crop at harvest time. And the Rio Grande that ran dry through a long stretch of the state was overflowing. The damp and stormy pattern is consistent with an El Niño year of above average Pacific storm activity. Soggy weather slogs off to the east From Colorado and across the Great Plains to Iowa, as much as 2 inches (5 centimeters) of rain fell Tuesday and into Wednesday, with some areas seeing even more. More storms were expected in Texas and Oklahoma after one in Amarillo, Texas, flooded streets and spawned a tornado Tuesday night. Storm totals in the Amarillo area topped 3.5 inches (9 centimeters). The weather was the remnant of tropical systems including Hurricane Polo, a Category 3 hurricane that made landfall overnight Monday on the Baja California peninsula and then farther inshore. In southern New Mexico, ongoing rain threatened to rot red chiles as the harvest wraps up. Mold and disease will put stress on the plants in the field, said Preston Mitchell, a Hatch Chile Association board member. “There will be nobody picking chile for at least five or six days,” Mitchell said. “All these growers whose fields were flooded, everything’s toast. Everything that’s out there is done.” But most of about 100 people who sought refuge from potential flooding in chile-growing Dona Ana County were headed home from shelters Wednesday, county officials said. As the weather cleared, water stopped spilling over an earthen flood-control structure in the area that held without failing. Acting Gov. Howie Morales declared a state of emergency that made $3.75 million available through local governments to help affected people get temporary housing, healthcare, food and transportation. Rachel is the latest in a busy Pacific hurricane season Mexican authorities remain on alert in the states of Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco due to Hurricane Rachel. In the state of Jalisco, schools were closed Wednesday in 30 municipalities as a precautionary measure. Rachel was located about 200 miles (320 km) west-southwest of Cabo Corrientes, Mexico. Its maximum sustained winds were around 90 mph (150 kmh), according to an advisory from the Miami-based National Hurricane Center. The cyclone was moving northwest at 7 mph (11 kph) and was forecast to turn toward the west-northwest and west later this week, moving away from mainland Mexico and passing south of the Baja California peninsula. The hurricane center said the Mexican government had discontinued all coastal watches and warnings. But it warned of possible isolated rainfall totals of up to 12 inches (30 centimeters) and heavy surf along the coasts of Guerrero, Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco states. In Jalisco, the bodies of three people — two children ages 3 and 15, and their mother — were found Sunday after the family went missing due to a river flooding in the city of Talpa de Allende, before Polo made landfall. The father is still missing, according to the Jalisco State Civil Protection agency. A tourist also is missing due to strong waves in Puerto Vallarta, but the agency says that case is not linked to Polo either. In the central Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Nolo threatened dangerous conditions for parts of Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument, a marine conservation area. Formerly a hurricane, the storm drenched parts of Hawaii’s Big Island over the weekend. Its maximum sustained winds were near 50 mph (85 kph).

articles.title: 7 candle warmers that deliver on scent without using a flame
articles.summary: We spoke with experts about how to use a candle warmer as a safer alternative to an open flame. Shop candle warmer lamps with auto shut-off and dimmable features.
articles.body: Lighting candles around your home is one of the easiest and fastest ways to create a relaxing ambiance. But candles can quickly become a fire safety hazard when not used properly. That’s where candle warmers can help. They’re a reliable, relatively safe alternative you can use to avoid those risks, especially if you often forget to put out candles before going to bed or leaving your home. Plus, candle warmers often come in the form of lamps, adding another source of light and decor to your space. To learn more about how to use a candle warmer lamp or plate safely, I spoke with a fire safety expert and a candle company owner, and rounded up highly-rated options from Amazon and other retailers. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our weekly newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. The best candle warmers of 2026 Nearly all of the candle warmers below have at least a 4.5-star average rating from 1,000 or more shoppers. This popular candle warmer lamp has a glass shade with ridges and comes in several colors, including clear, pink, beige and green. You can set it on a timer for two, four, eight or 10 hours and adjust the brightness four levels with the dial built into the power cable. It also includes a light bulb along with a spare. Shoppers love this candle warmer and say that they love that they can adjust the height on the lamp (which helps fit candles of different sizes). The Funistree flower candle lamp has a charming vintage feel, thanks to its petal-shaped shade. It comes with two halogen bulbs (though it only uses one at a time), and has a timer and dial you can use to dim the light. NBC Selected senior editor Shalwah Evans has tested this candle warmer and she loves that it melts candles slowly and evenly, offers good throw in a large space, and has a long cord so you can rest it on tall dressers. This candle warmer from Marycele, which has a wooden base, glass lampshade and halogen warming lightbulb, has a bit of a vintage look for anyone looking for that sort of decor. It also has a built-in timer and an electric dimmer that you can use to adjust the bulb’s brightness. Since the shade is glass, exercise caution when around it to avoid it breaking or shattering. This candle warming plate has a minimalist design and is the most affordable option on this list. It has a small red light on the bottom to let you know whether or not the warmer is on, and it automatically shuts off after eight hours, keeping you and your home safe. It isn’t a lamp, so it doesn’t provide additional light in your space and it offers the least amount of unique decor. This Maoyue candle warmer melts candle wax from the top down. It has a halogen bulb (comes with two) and a dimmable timer with two-, four- and eight-hour automatic shut off options to avoid overheating, according to the brand. It comes in a few colors and styles, including a lantern and a lamp. This candle warmer comes with a touch-button control that allows you to put it on a timer of either two, four or eight hours. It also has four levels of brightness so that you can control how quickly your candle burns, and it comes with two 50-watt halogen bulbs. It’s tall, so it’s compatible with candles of varying heights. This warmer heats candle wax using electrical heat and no light source. It’s compatible with jarred candles and individual wax melts that you place in the dish that sits inside the base. This way, you can control how much wax it burns at a time. The base has raised legs so it avoids coming in direct contact with (and heating) the surface below it for added safety. This monochromatic lamp is ideal for nearly all candle sizes due to the positioning and height of the light. The cord has a small dial that you can use to dim or brighten the light, allowing you to melt wax fast or slowly, and the base has four small holes on it to help heat ventilate from the bottom, according to the brand. How I picked the best candle warmers A candle warmer is a great option for anyone nervous about accidentally causing a fire in their space, says Teri Johnson, the founder of Harlem Candle Company. “It’s also a safer option, providing peace of mind if you occasionally forget to [blow out] a lit candle.” To help you find the best ones, I spoke with Johnson and other experts about what to consider when shopping and kept the following in mind when building this list: Safety: Most of the candle warmers on our list have an auto shut-off or timer feature, so there’s a backup in case you forget to turn it off. And since there is no open flame, it’s not as much of a risk as a lit candle that can be knocked down, says Jack Oehm, the battalion commander at the Fire Department of New York.Light/heat source: Many candle warmers require a halogen light bulb, which provides light and enough heat to gently melt a candle. The candle warmer lamps on this list come with a halogen bulb included, though others may require you to buy bulbs separately. The warmers that don’t require a bulb heat from the bottom. Size: Candles come in many sizes, so we included warmers with different heights and widths to fit varying candle options. Style and ambiance: In addition to functionality, we considered warmers with a range of styles for different tastes. Some look like vintage lanterns while others look like modern lamps or simple plates. How to use a candle warmer safely There are several safety precautions you should take when using a candle warmer to avoid causing a fire. Here’s what our experts recommend keeping in mind: Don’t leave it unattended. Regardless of whether you burn a candle traditionally or with a candle warmer, making sure you do so safely should always be a priority. An open flame is always a potential hazard because it can be knocked down by a pet or by someone moving in their sleep. That said, candle warmers themselves can also pose a threat when left unattended and used improperly, such as placing them too close to combustible decor or upholstery. When in doubt, review the brand’s safety tips before using. Place it in a safe area. Avoid common areas like the edge of an unstable nightstand or where there is flammable material, according to Oehm, where it may easily or accidentally fall or be knocked over by children or pets. Both the warmer and the candle become hot when in use so you shouldn’t try to handle or move the warmer, or especially the light source, while it’s hot. Instead, allow it to cool for a couple of hours. Don’t burn your candle simultaneously. You should never burn your candle while the warmer is on as it can lead to overheating, according to several of the brands mentioned above. Plus, it simply isn’t necessary since the light bulb is already melting the wax. Read the label. Always make sure to read labels and follow manufacturers instructions — they’ll usually have additional safety tips about proper bulb types and more. We also take steps to ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. articles.title: Billion-dollar power link connecting Israel to Europe hits roadblock in bitter regional feud
articles.summary: Cyprus accuses Recep Tayyip Erdoğan of blocking the Great Sea Interconnector energy project linking Israel, Cyprus and Greece amid maritime disputes.
articles.body: UNITED NATIONS — Cyprus Foreign Minister Constantinos Kombos accused Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan of "hypocritical and provocative" rhetoric over Gaza while warning that Ankara is trying to obstruct a major energy project linking Israel, Cyprus and Europe. "Turkey has been making threats and has been acting on threats against Cyprus, especially in the exclusive economic zone," Kombos told Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly. Kombos pointed to the Great Sea Interconnector, a planned subsea electricity cable linking Israel to Cyprus and Cyprus to Greece, connecting the island to Europe’s power grid. TRUMP'S AMBITIOUS ENERGY BET COULD BE A WINNING HAND AS THE WORLD BURNS MORE OIL, GAS THAN EVER "The main project of the electrical connection between Greece-Cyprus and then Cyprus-Israel has been blocked by Turkey because of illegal claims they have in terms of delimitation in the exclusive economic zone," Kombos said. The roughly €1.9 billion Great Sea Interconnector is designed to carry up to 1,000 megawatts across more than 1,200 kilometers of subsea cable. The EU has committed €657 million to the Cyprus-Crete section, which is intended to end Cyprus’ isolation from the European electricity system and eventually connect Israel more directly to the European market. TRUMP’S MIDDLE EAST ENERGY VICTORIES ARE A HUGE REMINDER OF AMERICA'S DOMINANCE The project has faced financial delays and geopolitical tensions tied to competing Greek and Turkish maritime claims in the Eastern Mediterranean. "The fact that we have someone challenging all the bases and all the norms of international law cannot be the answer to how we plan the future of our people," Kombos said. Those tensions also framed his sharp response to Erdoğan’s speech at the U.N. General Assembly. "We decided to stay in the room and hear Mr. Erdogan’s speech," Kombos said, referring to himself and Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides. "And we are both, at the same time, thinking that this is hypocritical and provocative." Kombos said Erdoğan’s appeals to the U.N. Charter stood in stark contrast to Turkey’s record on the divided Mediterranean island. "It’s an ongoing violation, an act of aggression, of invasion, of occupation," he said. "So it’s a very clear example of a distance between rhetoric and action, words and deeds." MIDDLE EAST TAKES CENTER STAGE AT UN AS REGIONAL LEADERS CONFRONT IRAN WAR, GAZA AND HOUTHI THREAT Erdoğan delivered a blistering attack on Israel during his Sept. 22 U.N. address, accusing the Israeli government of refusing to end its "occupation" and saying Gaza had become "the most inhumane and shameful concentration camp of our time." He also accused Israel of having a "genocidal mindset." Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations that it is committing genocide in Gaza. Cyprus has been divided since 1974, when a coup backed by Greece’s then-military junta was followed by a Turkish military intervention that left the island split. The internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus controls the south, while the northern third is administered by Turkish Cypriots with Turkey’s support. The self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus is recognized only by Turkey, and a U.N.-patrolled buffer zone separates the two sides. Efforts to reunify the island have repeatedly stalled. The U.N.-backed framework has centered on a bizonal, bicommunal federation, while Turkey has in recent years backed a two-state solution. Kombos said Cyprus wants negotiations to resume from where they broke down in 2017 but argued that progress ultimately depends on Ankara. "We need Turkey to give the green light to the Turkish Cypriot leadership," he said, adding that a two-state approach "runs contrary to everything this very organization and the United Nations Security Council have decided." The U.N. has recently stepped up efforts to revive the process. Secretary-General António Guterres traveled to Cyprus from July 28–29, meeting separately and jointly with Christodoulides and Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhürman in an effort to advance talks toward a "comprehensive and sustainable settlement." TRUMP COULD HAND PRIZED STEALTH JETS TO NATO ALLY ONCE SEEN AS ALLIANCE HEADACHE Kombos also raised concern over the possibility of Turkey obtaining U.S. F-35 fighter jets. "This is something that is of concern to us, of course, as well as to other countries in the region," he said. "We cannot just accept this as the usual day at the office. This is something that’s important. It’s upsetting regional balances." At the same time, Cyprus has moved significantly closer to Washington. Kombos said the U.S.-Cyprus relationship is "probably right now at the highest level we have ever been," pointing to strategic dialogue, military cooperation, joint exercises and work to make Cypriot facilities compatible with assets used by the U.S. and NATO partners. Earlier this month, Washington renewed Cyprus’ exemption from U.S. International Traffic in Arms Regulations restrictions for fiscal year 2027, allowing transfers of US defense articles and services. Cyprus is also eligible for U.S. Foreign Military Sales and the Excess Defense Articles program. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We want to make sure that we are an active, useful partner in the international system," Kombos said, arguing that Cyprus’ location and close ties with Israel, Gulf states, Europe and the US give it an increasingly important regional role.

articles.title: Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann gave modest boost to Belfast hotels
articles.summary: Official figures show that 189,000 hotel beds were sold, up almost 4% compared with August 2025.
articles.body:
The All Ireland Fleadh gave the Belfast hotel market a modest boost during August, initial survey data suggests.

Official figures suggest that an estimated 189,000 hotel beds were sold in the city, up almost 4% compared with 182,000 bed sales in August 2025.

Room occupancy rates in the city were up by two percentage points year-on-year, from 83% to 85%.

The Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann ran from 2 to 9 August - it was the first time the event had been held in Belfast.

In Northern Ireland as a whole, just under 470,000 beds were sold in August, compared with 447,000 in 2025, an increase of 5%.

People visiting Belfast for the Fleadh were not just staying in hotels.

Self-catering and student accommodation was used as well as a dedicated campsite.

The festival exceeded the organisers' expectations, with 1.6 million visits to the city recorded over eight days of celebrations.

More than 176,000 people were in the city centre on the day of the opening ceremony - an increase of 95% on the same day last year.

There were more than 200 events planned across the city, with live music sessions, dance classes and family fun days featuring in the programme.

The Fleadh's main outdoor stage was located outside Belfast City Hall and offered free live performances each day.

The biggest change for residents and visitors was the creation of a large pedestrianised zone in the city centre over the course of the festival to allow for performances and activities to take place.

articles.title: Iraq’s Kurdish forces look to a new era after US withdrawal
articles.summary: Peshmerga unification seeks stability, overcoming party disputes to build a national force in Iraq’s Kurdish landscape.
articles.body:
Iraq’s Kurdish forces are entering a new era following the withdrawal of US-led international forces that had been in the country to fight ISIL (ISIS).

On Wednesday, the United States announced the formal end of Operation Inherent Resolve, its name for the 12-year-long campaign to defeat ISIL, and the completion of the withdrawal of its military forces from Iraq.

Other partners in the war against the armed group also withdrew from Iraq, in accordance with a September 30 deadline set by Washington and Baghdad two years prior.

For years, Iraq’s Kurdish forces – known as the Peshmerga – have relied on close military support from coalition forces, and the US in particular, to safeguard their autonomy and defend against ISIL.

Their withdrawal has posed new political and security challenges for Iraq. Where does the Peshmerga stand today?

Days before the coalition’s withdrawal, on September 21, the Erbil-based Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) – which presides over Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdistan region – announced that it had finally merged Kurdish armed factions into a unified fighting force.

In his speech at the ceremony marking the event, KRG President Nechirvan Barzani characterised it as a major national step towards consolidating the region’s institutions.

“Kurdistan needs one force, one ministry, and one command,” he said. “The Peshmerga must be a national force, free from party interference and disputes. Today, we take a major step towards achieving this goal.”

Barzani announced that the militias affiliated with his Kurdish Democratic Party (KDP) and its historic rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) were now under one structure. The KDP and PUK represent the two dominant Kurdish Iraqi factions.

Zeidon Alkinani, a Middle East political analyst and founding director of the Doha-based Arab Perspectives Institute, told Al Jazeera that the unification would help stabilise Iraq.

“Iraq’s most damaging rivalries have been within communities, intra-Shia and intra-Kurdish, not between them,” he said.

He says reducing the role of the Erbil-based KDP and the Sulaymaniyah-based PUK party structures within the Peshmerga “strengthens Iraq’s stability and gives Erbil firmer legal footing with Baghdad”.

However, the work is far from finished. Barzani, in his speech, warned that the unification marked the start of a phase that “may be even more difficult” than past Kurdish struggles, requiring the Peshmerga to stand above party loyalties.

“The test is whether [unification] survives, given the persistence of two geographically distinct commands”, Alkinani says.

Retired Lieutenant General Jabbar al-Yawar, former secretary general of the Ministry of Peshmerga in the KRG, told Al Jazeera that these parties were embroiled in a number of political disputes, including governance of Kurdistan and relations with Baghdad.

These disputes, he says, could extend to military institutions if the forces remain tied to political parties.

On the ground, the Ministry of Peshmerga insists that its forces are ready for the new era.

Spokesperson Major General Othman Mohammed told Al Jazeera that the Peshmerga “has always been on full alert,” touting its role in repelling the ISIL in 2014 despite having limited means.

He pointed to the relationship between the Peshmerga and Iraq’s other security forces, noting that commanders from both sides enjoyed very good cooperation and coordination.

This coordination has become more important now that the international coalition has ended its mission, with Iraqis now relying on their own capabilities to detect and stop ISIL activity.

Despite this readiness, Mohammed Salih, a non-resident senior fellow at the US-based Foreign Policy Research Institute and an expert on Iraqi and regional affairs, says there is “considerable uncertainty and concern among Kurds surrounding the US withdrawal”.

Many are asking whether the departure of US troops means the end of Washington’s commitment to Kurdish security, he told Al Jazeera, given that the US has been “a key security guarantor for the Kurdistan region for the past three decades”.

Importantly, the US took with it key air defence systems when it withdrew, creating serious concern for Erbil, which has come under several drone and missile attacks since the start of the US war on Iran.

Erbil has signalled its intention to continue cooperating with Baghdad as before, under Iraq’s federalist framework.

The day after coalition forces withdrew, KDP leader and former KRG President Masoud Barzani touted “very strong coordination with the Iraqi federal government to confront any kind of threat or danger, whether it comes under the name of ISIS or any other name”.

In Baghdad, he backed the federal government’s efforts to fight corruption, disarm Iran-aligned militias and settle outstanding disputes with Erbil under the constitution.

Iraqi federalism and unity “depend on communication, coordination and respect for the rule of law among political parties, not on foreign troops”, Alkinani of the Arab Perspectives Institute said, in relation to the coalition withdrawal.

Baghdad faced a dilemma when Washington demanded it disarm Iran-aligned Iraqi armed groups. The armed groups refused, pointing to the US presence in Iraq even as it waged war on Iran.

The withdrawal may help the cause of federalism by removing this justification, he said, “but only if Iraqis replace it with dialogue and law rather than force”.

articles.title: Travelodge failed Maidenhead sex assault victim 'at every stage'
articles.summary: Room intrusions were still being reported at one-in-10 Travelodge hotels this summer, a review finds.
articles.body:
A woman who was sexually assaulted by a man given a key to her hotel room was "fundamentally failed" by Travelodge "at every stage", an independent review has found.

Barrister Paul Greaney KC said the chain's security policies at the time of the attack at its Maidenhead hotel in December 2022 were "not fit for the purpose of keeping guests safe".

He found guests were still not as safe as they should be, with room intrusions reported at nearly one-in-10 Travelodge hotels this summer, and no policy in place on violence against women and girls.

Travelodge apologised "unreservedly" to the woman. The review did credit the company with making changes since March.

Kyran Smith, who obtained the key by falsely claiming to be the woman's boyfriend, was jailed for seven-and-a-half years in January.

The review found he was handed the key less than three minutes after approaching the reception desk, by a receptionist who had received no training in key security.

Greaney said blame rested with Travelodge as an organisation rather than with individual staff, and a culture had developed in which room intrusions were regarded as "one of those things".

The woman emailed a complaint to Travelodge in January 2023, addressed to chief executive Jo Boydell and others.

The review concluded the email was handled by her office without her knowledge, and did not come to Boydell's attention until March 2026.

The woman's complaint was instead investigated by a manager who was himself criticised in it, and the customer services team offered her a refund for her night's stay, which she understood to be £30.

Boydell stepped down as chief executive in August following criticism over the company's handling of safety complaints. The review said she deserved credit for driving improvements from March.

The attack became national news in March after the woman contacted the BBC, saying the case raised serious questions about room security at Travelodge hotels.

Since then, dozens of people have shared experiences of strangers entering their rooms, including a domestic abuse victim whose abuser was given a key to her room at a Travelodge in London.

Then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer wrote to Boydell in March urging her to "seriously engage" with the government over security. Greaney was appointed to lead the review the following month.

The review makes 38 recommendations, including moving towards a system that requires guests to show ID to get a room key, which Travelodge has been trialling at some hotels since May.

It also calls for body-worn cameras for reception staff, better checks that staff have understood their training, and for housekeepers to always send guests to reception.

Greaney said Travelodge must "urgently" create a policy on violence against women and girls, drawn up with the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, and train all staff in it.

The review said changes made this year had been done quickly "albeit years too late" and its new key security policy would prevent a repeat of the Maidenhead attack if applied correctly.

But it found the policy was "not being applied with anything like sufficient consistency on the ground".

Mystery shoppers were able to get into rooms through housekeeping staff at all five hotels tested, including Maidenhead, without being sent to reception or asked for proof they were entitled to enter.

At three of the hotels, staff confirmed a guest was staying there, and at two, room numbers were said out loud at check-in. The Maidenhead hotel scored worst of the five.

Other recommendations included networked CCTV across the chain and key card-controlled access to all residential corridors.

Greaney said room intrusions were a problem across the hotel sector.

He praised the woman's courage and determination, saying the problems would have remained "beneath the surface" had she not shared her experience.

Freddie van Mierlo, the Liberal Democrat MP for Henley and Thame, where Travelodge is based, said he was worried the company was "still trying to do safety on the cheap".

He said the review's recommendations would require "significant capital investment", and Travelodge needed to make clear it was prepared to deliver that.

Ray Reidy, Travelodge's interim chief executive, said the review made clear there were failures in its policies and in the way customers had been treated.

"I apologise unreservedly on behalf of Travelodge to all guests where we have failed," he said.

"We have made significant progress in preventing and addressing these issues over the past six months, and we recognise we still have further to go."

Travelodge said a new board committee would oversee the changes, with independent assessments of its progress after six and 12 months.

articles.title: Screaming, panicking, blood: Passengers detail horrifying Israel-bound flight
articles.summary: TEL AVIV — A stabbing, an emergency alert, a terrifying mid-air plunge.
articles.body: TEL AVIV — A stabbing, an emergency alert, a terrifying mid-air plunge. Details are still emerging after an Israel-bound flight carrying some 180 people emitted a distress signal Wednesday, raising fears of a possible hijacking when one pilot stabbed the other in the cockpit. Aviatar Alevi, who was onboard the Flydubai flight Wednesday, described people “screaming, running, panicking, blood.” “At the start I thought it was a plane malfunction, but then I started hearing screaming about the stabbings,” Alevi, 17, told NBC News. “Then I understood the weight of the actual situation.” “We didn’t know what was going to happen,” he said, adding that the possibility of death “was definitely an option.” The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, one of its rudders damaged, apparently by the force of its descent. The passengers, who had been flying from Dubai before the crisis, were mobbed by media and flag-waving fellow Israelis after finally arriving at Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport. They said they had feared for their lives after the plane plunged more than 14,000 feet in the span of 29 seconds at one point, according to FlightRadar24. “Imagine sitting on the plane, all scared after you fell down five kilometers. You don’t understand anything,” 16-year-old Peleg Itali told NBC News. Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, was recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia on Thursday as the other pilot, so far identified only as an Omani citizen, was being interrogated elsewhere in the country. Machchhar was widely praised for his efforts to prevent the plane from crashing, opening the cockpit door and allowing passengers and crew to rush in. Few details had emerged about the pilot as of Thursday morning. Questions about a possible motive, including whether it was terrorism-related, hang over the attack. “I don’t think it was a hijacking. It looks like a suicide attempt, simply because of what this hero, Yaniv, has described,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on “CBS Evening News,” as he praised Yaniv Hayun, who rushed into the cockpit and subdued the attacker. Hayun, who was pictured with his shirt spattered with blood sitting next to Netanyahu, said that he had confronted the pilot who had initiated the attack, according to the Israeli government press office. “I grabbed the attacker, and choked him, pulled him out first,” Hayun said. “I started pulling the controls.” “Thank God, we pulled it off. We really put our heads together and worked as a team,” Hayun said, adding: “It was between fear and a sense of a do-or-die situation.” “We had to win. We had to pull through and come out on top,” he said. Hayun told Netanyahu that he had acted based on what he’d seen on a TV show and helped stabilize the plane. Flydubai said on-duty crew who were onboard the flight were able to land the plane. Motive under investigation Netanyahu said it was still too early to determine why the pilot apparently stabbed his colleague and appeared to try to take over the Flydubai flight, and whether there was any Iranian involvement. “We’ve had signs that Iran, in particular through its proxies, was intending to heighten terrorist attacks against Israel and Israeli nationals abroad,” he said. “But I think it’s too early to say whether there was Iranian collusion here.” Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, meanwhile, branded the incident a “jihadist terrorist attack attempt,” without expanding on how he reached that conclusion. President Donald Trump also weighed in, calling it “an incredible story.” “It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job, and he stabbed the pilot,” Trump told reporters. All the passengers were Israeli, according to Netanyahu’s office. Four were dual American-Israeli citizens, two U.S. officials told NBC News. With few details on the suspect or on any potential motive surrounding the incident, Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for Netanyahu’s office said there was a “strong opinion” that the incident was a terror attack “but we can’t be sure until we debrief everybody.” An investigation by Saudi authorities is ongoing, David Mencer, a spokesperson for the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office, separately said. A senior U.S. official briefed on the Israeli investigation and a Saudi official also briefed on the probe said the stabbing increasingly looks like an act of terrorism based on early findings. The United Arab Emirates’ Attorney-General, Dr. Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, separately ordered an investigation into the incident. His office said the probe would seek to “gather information and evidence, establish the facts and circumstances of the incident, and determine the underlying motives,” in addition to examining “whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose, or involved any prior planning or direction.” Hessa Alyahya, spokesperson for the Saudi Embassy in the U.S., said authorities were waiting to determine whether the attack was a dispute between the pilots or whether it was an act sponsored by Iran or the Houthis. Israel and Saudi Arabia do not have official diplomatic relations.

articles.title: What happened in failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
articles.summary: The convicted killer is in hospital in Tennessee after surviving two lethal injections, in a case that has raised many questions.
articles.body:
US convicted murderer Christa Pike is in hospital and being given "life-saving measures" after Tennessee authorities failed in their attempt to execute her by lethal injection.

The case of Pike, whose attempted execution had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, has raised a number of questions.

These include what went went wrong, what happens next, and - for opponents of the death penalty - fresh concerns around the suffering of an inmate when an execution does not go to plan.

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, an attack that was perpetrated alongside her then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp.

She was scheduled to be put to death on Wednesday evening, local time. The injections were allowed by the US Supreme Court at the eleventh hour after the legal battle.

Pike was given two syringes of the drug pentobarbital, though her legal team said these failed to stop her heartbeat and that she could still be heard snoring.

US death row inmate survives execution attempt after two lethal injections

The Tennessee Department of Correction defended the method it used, and said "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening".

The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.

Authorities have yet to provide their explanation of why the dosage given to Pike proved to be non-fatal, although medical experts have provided theories of their own.

Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine who told the BBC he had been retained by Pike's legal team as a medical expert, said she probably never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause apnoea and cardiovascular failure.

The state correction department added that Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility.

One of her lawyers said she was "being provided life-saving measures" in hospital.

Her health status is unclear as of Thursday morning.

In his emailed comments to the BBC, Zivot said: "It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury."

A third-party review has been ordered by the state governor, Bill Lee, who also says the year's last remaining execution will not go ahead as planned.

May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who had pushed for Pike's execution to take place, told NBC News the events had been "a mess".

Opponents of the death penalty have similarly been quick to react.

Maya Foa, the chief executive of international legal organisation Reprieve, said: "We cannot know exactly what went wrong, because so much happened behind a curtain – lethal injection relies on secrecy at every stage, to hide the violence of the state taking a human life."

Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. There is a historical precedent of authorities making a second attempt to execute those on death row.

Meanwhile Shipp, Pike's boyfriend and co-defendant, remains in prison, having been spared the death penalty under state law. He was 17 at the time that Slemmer was killed.

Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.

Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review - which took place under the presidency of Joe Biden - raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".

His government banned its use in federal executions but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.

Why the death penalty is on the rise in US

In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.

The Tennessee Department of Correction has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded". Drugs may degrade for a number of reasons, including if it has aged beyond its use-by date and its potency has decreased.

The department issued a broader defence of its method, writing in a statement: "The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective."

The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.

The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal injection. He was given a one-year reprieve by Governor Bill Lee.

More widely across the US, the issue of botched executions continues to cause alarm.

In 2022, more than a third of executions in the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPI) - an organisation that provides statistics and research on the death penalty but does not take a stance on it morally.

The DPI says lethal injection has the high­est rate of botched exe­cu­tions.

An incident in Oklahoma in 2014 gained particular notoriety. The execution of Clayton Lockett was postponed after 20 minutes because the lethal injection of three drugs failed to work properly when one of his veins ruptured, and he went on to writhe and shake uncontrollably.

In the US, 27 of the 50 states have the death penalty under state law. The federal government can also carry out executions after President Donald Trump, a supporter of capital punishment, ended a moratorium last year, However, it is yet to actually carry out any executions since then.

articles.title: Christa Pike execution fails: What next when a lethal injection is botched?
articles.summary: Only woman on Tennessee ‘death row’ is in hospital after two injections failed to kill her.
articles.body:
Two doses of a lethal injection drug have failed to kill Christa Gail Pike , a 50-year-old woman who was due to be executed on Wednesday. Pike was taken to hospital after it was found that her heart was still beating following the procedure.

Pike would have been the first woman in more than 200 years to be put to death in Tennessee and was the only woman on the state’s death row. Her attempted execution with doses of the sedative pentobarbital went ahead despite a last-minute stay by a federal appeals court on Wednesday, which was overturned just an hour before her execution by the Supreme Court.

Human rights experts said the botched execution illustrates why the death penalty is inhumane and should be abolished.

Clive Stafford Smith, a human rights lawyer who has represented many American death row inmates as well as detainees held at the notorious Guantanamo Bay detention centre, told Al Jazeera: “I’ve been in the execution chamber with six of my clients and it’s never the clinical process they’d have you believe. And it’s always a desperate midnight struggle to stop it.”

He added: “In the end, you have to question whether this makes the world a better, more civilised place. Why, indeed, do we kill people to prove that killing people is wrong?”

Ahead of the planned execution, Morris Tidball-Binz, the UN special rapporteur on arbitrary executions, told the UK’s Times newspaper: “If executed, Christa Pike would be a victim of torture to death. This will be a gross violation of human rights.”

Here’s what we know about what happens when an execution goes wrong.

Pike was found guilty of the murder of another young woman she had viewed as a romantic rival, when she was aged 18, more than 30 years ago.

In January 1995, Pike, her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson lured Colleen Slemmer, 19, into a wooded area and tortured and killed her. All four were students at a Job Corps vocational centre in Knoxville.

The case attracted huge public interest, especially after it was revealed that the attackers had carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest, which Shipp later admitted to doing. Pike, who delivered the killing blow to the victim’s head, smashing her skull, kept a piece of Slemmer’s skull afterwards.

Pike and Shipp confessed and were convicted of first-degree murder in 1996. Pike was sentenced to death; Shipp, who was 17 at the time and therefore ineligible for the death penalty, received life with the possibility of parole.

Her case is highly unusual in that she is a woman and was a teenager when she carried out the murder. Other death row inmates who were convicted at the age of 18 – all men – have had their sentences commuted to life in prison without parole.

“Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions,” her lawyers wrote. They also argued that Pike had been the victim of appalling childhood abuse – including two rapes when she was aged 11 and 17.

Stafford Smith told Al Jazeera: “Very few women are executed, but fewer still in Tennessee – it has been 200 years. So, this is a step back to about 1820. Christa was just a teenager, and had undergone horrendous abuse as a child. Now she is 50, a totally different person. It is so pointless – will this really make the world a more civilised place?”

Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, however, has spoken out in support of the execution.

On Wednesday, a federal court temporarily put the planned execution on hold, on legal and technical grounds. But an hour before the midnight deadline for her execution was to expire, the US Supreme Court overruled the stay on her execution, paving the way for jail authorities to proceed.

Pike had asked to be shot by an all-female firing squad instead of by lethal injection, which she said she feared would be too painful.

Her lawyers had also argued that the injection would be torturous for her as she has “small veins”. This request was denied, however.

Following the Supreme Court’s order to go ahead with the execution, Pike was administered two doses of the sedative pentobarbital at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, Tennessee, on Wednesday evening, according to media witnesses.

From outside the prison, The Associated Press journalist Kim Chandler reported that, initially, when the injections were administered, Pike appeared noticeably awake.

“The blinds were closed for the first time to the execution chamber at 7:46pm (23:46 GMT), they opened again at 7:49pm (23:49 GMT),” Chandler said.

“Her mouth fell open a few times, and she began to loudly snore. She gasped a few times,” she noted.

“The curtain to the execution chamber closed for the final time at 8:06pm (00:06 GMT), and she could be heard loudly snoring, clearly very alive, in the chamber until media witnesses were told to leave the area at about 8:53pm (00:53 GMT),” Chandler added.

The Tennessee Department of Correction did not immediately explain why the execution had not been completed.

According to NBC News, late on Wednesday, Pike’s lawyers had filed a federal court motion during the process seeking again to halt her execution, citing witnesses’ accounts that “executioners had injected both syringes of lethal injection chemicals and Pike is still alive and snoring”.

“Ms Pike has not lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat and is audibly snoring,” they said, according to the court documents seen by the media.

Her lawyers also told US media that while she was being treated at a hospital, she needed “immediate medical care”.

Tennessee authorities have not explained this yet.

However, Stafford Smith, who has attended several executions in support of clients in the past, told Al Jazeera that there are two probable reasons why the injection failed to kill Pike.

“The first is that the drugs were probably out of date. Something that we’ve been observing a lot for the last 10 years is that they administer drugs that are no longer valid,” he said.

Stafford Smith noted that there is, however, a valid reason for this, which is that drug companies make sedatives like pentobarbital to help people and save lives and are often opposed to their drugs being used to execute people.

“So the states have a real problem getting drugs to kill people and they’ve gone to extraordinary extents with very unreliable providers. So you can suspect that they just had an invalid batch of drugs in Pike’s case,” Smith explained.

“The other thing about Pike is that, as is very common with people who end up in her situation, they’ve been through a lot of abuse and drug abuse. So it might have been very hard to find her veins and get a needle into it. Moreover, doctors are also not allowed to take part in this process in the US. So they have incompetent people administering such drugs, which could have resulted in the injection failing,” he added.

Defending its handling of the case, the Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement late on Wednesday that the agency had “followed every step of the state’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office”.

“The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility,” the statement concluded.

At the moment, it is unclear, as Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has paused all remaining 2026 executions in the state following Wednesday’s incident with Pike and has called for a comprehensive, third-party review. She is currently in hospital. She may return to death row, but Stafford Smith said this is uncertain.

Yes. Botched executions do happen but the frequency varies substantially by method, according to data compiled by legal scholar Austin Sarat and the Death Penalty Information Center.

In his 2014 book, Gruesome Spectacles: Botched Executions and America’s Death Penalty, Sarat noted that from 1890 to 2010, 8,776 people were executed in the US and 276 of those executions (3.15 percent) went wrong in some way. Sarat also noted that lethal injection was the method that had the highest rate of botched executions at 7.2 percent in this period.

Previous botched lethal injection cases include the case of murderer Alva Campbell in November 2017 in Ohio. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, “the execution team first worked on both of Alva Campbell’s arms for about 30 minutes.. while he was on a gurney in the state’s death chamber and then tried to find a vein in his right leg below the knee. … About 80 minutes after the execution was scheduled to begin, the 69-year-old Campbell shook hands with two guards after it appeared the insertion was successful.”

“About two minutes later … Gary Mohr, head of the Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction … called off the execution after talking with the medical team, [saying] ‘It was my decision that it was not likely that we’re going to access veins.’” But a few months later, in March, 2018, Campbell died on death row due to terminal medical conditions.

“Botched executions have happened many times. I’ve had six of my clients executed over the years. Two were with the gas chamber, two with the electric chair and two with lethal injection, and there’s almost always some form of botching,” Stafford Smith said.

“But it’s just an uncivilised process carried out by people who are pretty uncivilised,” he added.

articles.title: Exclusive: New church campaign says America's family crisis won't be solved by politics, but by pastors
articles.summary: Communio's JP De Gance says unmarried people in their 30s are the loneliest demographic and urges churches to actively encourage marriage now.
articles.body: America's birthrate has fallen to just 1.57 births per woman, a level that one Christian leader warns could reshape the nation's future if the trend continues. "For every 200 people in a population, they'll be replaced by only 157," Communio founder and President J.P. De Gance told Fox News Digital. "We're at the cusp of a major civilizational bottleneck." Now, Communio is launching a nationwide "Family and Civilization" campaign, obtained first by Fox News Digital, urging churches to take a more active role in strengthening marriages and families. FAMILY BREAKDOWN IN PENNSYLVANIA PROMPTS FAITH-BASED EFFORT TO BRING MARRIAGE BACK The initiative argues that churches, not government, have historically helped rebuild family life during periods of societal decline and can do so again by encouraging healthy relationships before they reach crisis. "Our message to churches is we should be helping," De Gance said. "Our young people know this, right? We shouldn't be talking to our kids more frequently about a great college, a great career over and above. These are good things, but they shouldn't be spoken of in exclusion to seeking and being intentional about relationships." According to De Gance, the loneliest and unhappiest segment of the population are unmarried young people. "And the reality is, the loneliest people in America right now are not the elderly and are not the widow, it's the unmarried in their 30s are disproportionately the most likely to say that they're lonely," De Gance said. "And if parents understood that this means that their kids are more likely to die 15 years shorter — that's what the public health data says — they would be probably sharing a different message to their kids in youth, in high school, in those college years and to be intentional with their relationships in their 20s." 1 IN 6 ADULTS PLAGUED BY LONELINESS AS RESEARCHERS REVEAL LASTING IMPACT OF COVID PANDEMIC In addition to churches encouraging marriage, De Gance said it is also on parents to encourage their children, as marriage is often the last thing prioritized when it comes to a child’s future career and life decisions. "Nine out of 10 parents say it's important that their kids have a fulfilling career, but only 2 in 10 or 1 in 5 parents say it's important that their kids get married, and only 1 in 5 say it's important that their kids have children, right," De Gance said. "Now the reality is, our kids, our young people, are actually doing what they're being taught to do. That they're seeking material well-being over and above these enduring, lifelong goods of close connection through marriage and family. What we're hoping to do is inspire churches to cast vision positively around marriage and family," he said. A 2023 study from Pew Research found nearly half the parents who responded to the survey said that it is not very important or not important at all to them for their kids to marry, or even have kids themselves. AOC FROZE HER EGGS AT 36. HERE’S WHAT MY GENERATION GOT WRONG ABOUT MOTHERHOOD Being financially independent, having careers, and earning a college degree ranked much higher for parents than their kids getting married or having children. Part of their ask to churches and pastors, De Gance said, is to encourage churches to talk about marriage more. "Look, 85% of all churches spend nothing in the area of marriage and relationship ministry. Ninety-one percent have nothing for singles," DeGance said. "But one thing they can do this Sunday and in future Sundays is always talk aspirationally, preach aspirationally about the beauty of Christian marriage, help folks, aspire to it, lay out that great mystery that the Apostle Paul talks about in Ephesians 5, that human marriage is actually the symbol, the sign of Christ's sacrificial love for his bride, the church? And that's something a church can do right now, so that our young people are always thinking about it. And aspire to it, and then provide the practical guidance to be able to seek it out," he said. CHASTITY BEFORE MARRIAGE? NO COHABITATION? DATA SAYS COUPLES WHO SKIP BOTH MAY HAVE STRONGER UNIONS Another thing churches can do, De Gance said, is to bring young people together, both inside and outside of church, in order to help spur more marriages. "We can become a lot more strategic after that, where we're creating environments where people meet in real life. We should not abdicate our responsibility to technology and dating apps, right," he said. "Church should be a venue where young people meet, form community, have fun outside of spiritual and faith formation. The local church used to be the hub for civic life. And it's our message that given the loneliness and isolation, the church is perfectly positioned, to be that hub once again." He said he holds on to hope that society will be reminded of the beauty of marriage by witnessing it. "At some point, there will be a major rebound. I'm filled with hope, and I'm also an optimist that those who grasp the great good of married life and seek the happiness that's most frequently found in it. These are the folks that are most likely to marry, the most likely to have kids. It's going to bring about a significant renewal and revival in the West.
