articles.body: Tennessee failed to execute the lone woman on its death row after two lethal injections. Undecided voters weigh their options ahead of next month’s elections. And details emerge from inside the near-catastrophic Flydubai flight bound for Israel. Here’s what to know today. Tennessee fails to execute inmate after 2 lethal injections Tennessee failed to execute the lone woman on its death row as planned yesterday, even after twice injecting her with a lethal drug. Attorneys for Christa Pike said last night that she was being treated at a hospital, but they did not know her condition. Pike, 50, was convicted of murdering a classmate in 1995. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. Journalists who witnessed the attempted execution described snoring and complaints from Pike about pain. At times, the curtain was closed and they could only hear sounds. Pike was heard saying, “My arm feels like it’s about to burst open,” according to one journalist. In an interview with NBC News this morning, the mother of victim Colleen Slemmer, May Martinez, described the attempt as “a mess.” Gov. Bill Lee ordered a review of the failed execution, the second in Tennessee this year. Earlier in the day, the Supreme Court stepped in to allow the state to put Pike to death, overturning a lower court ruling that had halted the move. She was set to be the first female in more than 200 years that the state had put to death, according to historical records. Read the full story of the failed execution here. Here’s what else to know about Pike’s case. Cornell student’s 2024 statement to police reveals new details about night of alleged rape The Cornell student who alleged in a lawsuit that she was raped and plied with drugs at a frat house in 2024 described the incident to police in a sworn statement, according to the document, which was obtained by NBC News. “I would say that it was the most intoxicated I’ve ever been in my life,” she told police. “I felt like I was unable to make any decisions.” Her statement mirrored many of the allegations in the lawsuit. She described going to the Chi Phi fraternity house. There, a friend asked whether she was interested in a threesome, which she said she agreed to. At one point during the night, “multiple men walked into the room,” and, she told police, “I was instantly horrified.” She ran across the room to hide under the covers of another bed, the statement said, which she said felt like the only option because they were standing between her and the exit. Here’s what else was detailed. How 16 undecided voters are weighing their 2026 election options In a national NBC News poll, 5% of voters said they weren’t sure which party they wanted to see controlling Congress after this year’s elections. Our reporters spoke with 16 of these undecided voters to understand what’s important to them as they decide who to elect this fall. Here are some of the top takeaways: 💵 Costs dominate: Almost every voter said high costs are top of mind, including the price of medicine, groceries and gas. “I’m eating less food because I can only afford so much,” one said. 🗳️ Down on both parties: Voters feel little loyalty to either party — and many of them said that’s in part because they aren’t sure either understands what’s important to them. 🏛️ Concerns with Trump: Several voters — including those who backed Trump in 2024 — voiced concerns about his handling of the economy and the Iran war. Read the full story here. For subscribers: James Talarico once took a vow to refuse campaign donations from people representing industries tied to coal, oil or natural gas. Now, locked in a high-stakes contest for a Senate seat in Texas, he has drifted from that promise. Screaming, panicking, blood: Passengers detail horrifying Israel-bound flight A pilot stabbed his co-pilot aboard a plane headed to Israel yesterday and may have tried to crash the aircraft with 174 people on board, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said. The pilot who initiated the attack is an Omani citizen and is being interrogated in Saudi Arabia, he added. Israeli officials also praised the stabbed pilot, identified as Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, for his actions in opening the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to rush in, secure the cockpit and prevent the plane from crashing. “He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals,” Netanyahu said. “I wish Captain Machchhar a speedy and full recovery. He is a true hero.” “I grabbed the attacker, and choked him, pulled him out first,” passenger Yaniv Hayun told Netanyahu in a face-to-face meeting, according to the Israeli government press office. Hayun, a plumber, said he entered the cockpit and subdued the attacker. “I started pulling the controls.” Hayun told Netanyahu that he took actions based on what he had seen on a TV show and helped stabilize the plane. Netanyahu said a motive was being determined, including whether it was an attempt to commit an act of terrorism. He said he expected the pilot who initiated the attack would be moved to Dubai soon. A senior U.S. official and a Saudi official said the stabbing increasingly looks like an act of terrorism based on the early results from the investigation. Here’s what else we know about the flight. articles.body: CANTON TOWNSHIP, Mich. — The parents of a Detroit-area toddler who pulled a loaded pistol out of his backpack at a daycare will face charges in the case, police said Wednesday. In a statement, police in Canton Township said the parents would make an initial court appearance Thursday. The Wayne County prosecutor’s office declined to offer details or additional comment, saying it would wait until a judge signs off on the charges. No one was injured Monday when the boy held a gun in a holster at Childrens World Early Learning Center. Canton Police Chief Joseph Bialy praised a staff member for their quick and safe intervention. One of the child’s parents is a police officer in the Detroit area, Bialy said earlier this week, though the gun was not described as a work firearm. The chief said it was “shocking” to see a video of the boy handling the gun. “The video is hard to watch, but I’m comforted by the fact that nobody was injured,” Bialy told reporters. Under Michigan law, firearms must be locked up at home when children are present. The penalties depend on the facts of each case, but they are greatly enhanced if a gun is fired and someone is wounded or killed. A man from Newaygo County is serving more than three years in prison after his 5-year-old grandson was fatally shot by another child who got access to a shotgun.

articles.title: UAE investigates possible ‘terrorist’ link in attack on flight to Israel
articles.summary: Investigators will probe whether incident was linked to any ‘terrorist activity or intent’, UAE state media reports.
articles.body:
The United Arab Emirates’ chief prosecutor has launched an investigation into the cockpit fight on board a Flydubai flight to Israel , which forced the plane to be diverted and land in Saudi Arabia.

Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi has formed a team of public prosecutors to investigate the midair altercation between the two pilots on board Flydubai flight FZ1073, Emirati state news agency WAM reported on Thursday.

The flight was travelling from Dubai International Airport to Tel Aviv on Wednesday before being diverted and landing safely at Tabuk airport in Saudi Arabia.

Investigators will examine the circumstances and motives behind the incident, and whether it was linked to any “terrorist activity or intent” or involved prior planning or direction, WAM reported.

Al Shamsi said UAE judicial authorities have jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft is registered in the UAE and flies under its flag, adding that UAE law applies to crimes committed on board “even if they occur outside the country’s territory”.

Earlier, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he spoke with the UAE’s president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who agreed that Israel would “join the interrogation” of the suspect.

Netanyahu has credited the Flydubai pilot, Indian national Smit Machchhar, as well as passengers, with averting catastrophe, after a co-pilot allegedly stabbed him and tried to crash the plane.

Israeli passengers on the aircraft carrying 174 people described how the injured Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door to let them in before they wrestled with the co-pilot and stabilised the plane during a descent so sharp that the rudder of the jet was ripped off.

“We felt helpless, suspended in midair, and I didn’t know who to turn to. But it was all instinct to survive,” one of the responders, Asaf Rajuan, said in a new statement shared by Israel’s presidency.

Israel’s foreign ministry said the people on board were from Israel, India and the UAE. The US State Department said four passengers had US citizenship.

Flydubai has said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended.

articles.title: How was the Flydubai pilot who attacked his co-pilot cleared to fly?
articles.summary: The Flydubai scare has raised several questions for Israel and the civil aviation industry.
articles.body:
The diversion of a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv following a pilot brawl has raised questions about the pilot vetting process and aviation security.

Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Wednesday said that the flight captain, who was stabbed by the co-pilot, managed to open the cockpit door. He dubbed the captain, Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, “a true hero” for preventing “a catastrophic midair disaster”.

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has ordered an investigation into the incident. The investigation team would “collect information and evidence to determine the truth of the incident, its circumstances, details, and motives, and to verify the extent of its connection to any terrorist activity or purpose, or the existence of prior planning or direction for it”, the UAE’s Attorney General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi said on Thursday.

Saudi Arabia has yet to provide updates regarding the incident.

At this point, there are more questions than answers about the Flydubai incident. So, how was the alleged attacker allowed to fly, and what do we know about the pilot he stabbed?

At about 8:44 local time, nearly two and a half hours after takeoff from Dubai, the distress call came in.

The captain and his co-pilot were allegedly engaged in fighting as the aircraft swiftly lost altitude, dropping from 33,000 feet (10,000 metres) to 17,000 feet (5,000 metres) within a minute, according to Israeli officials.

Netanyahu said that one of the pilots had stabbed the other and then tried to crash the plane.

A wounded Machchhar somehow managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to gain entry and overpower the alleged attacker, Israeli media reported.

The crew available on the flight were able to take control of the aircraft – and safely land it an hour later in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

Both pilots were injured in the fighting and were being treated in Saudi Arabia.

What we know about the pilot who allegedly attacked his colleague

Very little verified information has come through so far.

After initial treatment, he was taken into custody by authorities in Saudi Arabia, but has not been charged yet. No official confirmation has come out regarding his citizenship.

There is no information so far on his flying hours, qualifications or whether he had flown to Israel before on a Flydubai aeroplane, where he was reportedly employed less than a year ago.

While some Israeli officials rushed to call it a “jihadist attack,” Netanyahu has said that “it’s too early to say,” whether this was a targeted attack or one with an Iranian role. He also added that any motive behind the alleged attack was not clear.

“I think he’ll be taken to the Emirates, where he comes from, or at least where he left, where he flew off from, and we’ll be following and possibly also participating in this investigation,” Netanyahu told Fox News in an interview.

The initial statements from the airline and Saudi authorities say that investigations are continuing and people should refrain from speculation.

Flydubai is a UAE operator, whose certification and operational oversight fall under the UAE’s General Civil Aviation Authority (GCAA).

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency told Reuters that Flydubai’s certification and safety oversight rest with the GCAA. “This includes responsibility for ensuring that the operator meets the applicable requirements concerning its flight crews and their fitness to fly,” EASA said.

The standard GCAA regulatory framework requires a valid professional pilot’s licence, the appropriate aircraft type rating, a current Class 1 medical certificate and English language proficiency alongside required flight experience.

The Class 1 medical process covers physical and mental health; pilots with relevant psychiatric conditions, substance misuse, or other specified concerns can be referred for further assessment before being declared fit.

“Pilot vetting is very thorough, from security and financial checks to mental health evaluation,” said Saj Ahmad, the chief analyst at StrategicAero Research, a London-based aviation consultancy.

“But those checks are a single snapshot in time and will never uncover whether a person has issues that then manifest in the workplace or flight deck,” he told Al Jazeera.

“This is why it’s so hard to know what people think and what they may do if they feel a sense of some form of injustice,” Ahmad added.

Israeli media has pressed on with claims, quoting the Transport Minister Miri Regev, that an agreement with the UAE mandates that only pilots holding passports from countries with diplomatic relations with Israel may land in the country. Al Jazeera could not verify this claim.

Israel’s Ministry of Transport Security Department’s description of its responsibilities includes “security screening of foreign flights crossing/landing in Israel” and directing security arrangements for air transport services. It does not specify routine individual background vetting of commercial airline pilots or cabin crew.

Now, Israel says it would ramp up security checks on pilots flying into the country. “Every pilot that is going to be flying into Israel, we are going to know the pilots’ identities, know who they are, and do some type of security check,” Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the Israeli prime minister’s office, said.

Machchhar, hailed as a hero by prime ministers of Israel and India, hails from a suburb in Mumbai and currently lives in Dubai with his wife and two kids.

Currently, he is recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk.

Machchhar managed to activate the release to open the cockpit door, according to Israeli officials, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the co-pilot.

Machchhar worked with Indian commercial airline SpiceJet for more than a decade before joining Flydubai in 2022, his LinkedIn profile says. He has logged nearly 9,750 flying hours over a career spanning about 15 years.

After school, he enrolled in a textile engineering course with the aim of continuing the family’s business before pursuing management studies at Mumbai’s Welingkar Institute of Management.

It was there, at an aviation seminar, that he discovered flying when he was about 19 years old.

Machchhar later trained in New Zealand before joining SpiceJet, where he spent 11 years. He has been with Flydubai for four years.

“Delay is not my problem. As long as you’re walking out of the aircraft is what I want,” Machchhar said in a podcast in 2025 on a YouTube channel. “When I get out of the cockpit or the aircraft, I don’t want the other guy to know that I’m a pilot,” he said.

“When I wear the uniform, then no nonsense and just do your job, finish the job. When you walk out of the cockpit, that’s it. Stop thinking about that. Someone else needs you now. The kids are there. They want to play with you,” he had said.

There have been few instances of deliberate violence inside flights.

The kind of “violence in the flight deck can vary, but often the strategy is to open the door so that other crew members can assist,” Ahmad of StrategicAero Research told Al Jazeera.

“Sadly, these real-time events are hard to predict and harder to bring under control. The Flydubai event yesterday was unique in that other flight crew were on hand to land the airplane,” he said, referring to crew who were reportedly flying as passengers before taking on the return flight as crew.

“It’s frightening to think of what the outcome would have been if those additional pilots were not there to take control,” Ahmad added.

Japan Airlines Flight 350, 1982: Captain Seiji Katagiri deliberately pushed the airplane into a dive and activated thrust reversers on approach to Tokyo. The first officer countered his control inputs while the flight engineer physically restrained the captain. The aircraft crashed short of Haneda, killing 24 of 174 people on board. Katagiri was later ruled not guilty by reason of insanity.

Pacific Southwest Airlines Flight 1771, 1987: A disgruntled former employee, travelling as a passenger, shot his former supervisor and members of the flight crew. The aircraft subsequently entered a fatal dive. All 43 people on board died.

FedEx Flight 705, 1994: Off-duty FedEx employee Auburn Calloway, travelling in the cockpit jump seat, attacked the three-person flight crew with a hammer and other weapons in an attempt to seize the aircraft. The crew fought him and landed safely in Memphis.

Germanwings Flight 9525, 2015: First officer Andreas Lubitz locked the captain out of the cockpit and deliberately flew the A320 into the French Alps, killing all 150 people on board. France’s BEA found that the medical-certification system failed to prevent a pilot experiencing a serious mental disorder from exercising his licence.

China Eastern Flight MU5735, 2022: The US National Transportation Safety Board data released this year shows both engine fuel switches were manually moved to CUTOFF before the Boeing 737-800’s fatal dive. But China has not published a final investigation establishing exactly who made the inputs or why. All 132 on board died.

articles.title: Sacred pages of 1,000-year-old gospel reveal ancient DNA scientists never expected
articles.summary: The York Gospels, a 1,000-year-old manuscript, revealed ancient sheeppox virus DNA preserved in its parchment pages, stunning researchers worldwide.
articles.body: Scientists recently discovered traces of an ancient disease in an unlikely place: the pages of a 1,000-year-old gospel book. The discovery, which centered on the York Gospels, was announced by University College Dublin (UCD) in early September. In a study recently published in Science Advances, UCD researchers traced thousands of years of evolution of the sheeppox virus using ancient DNA preserved in manuscripts and animal remains. DAMAGED FRAGMENT DEEMED 'UNREMARKABLE' TURNS OUT TO BE RARE PIECE OF HOMER'S 'ODYSSEY' HISTORY The highly contagious disease affects sheep but is not known to infect humans. Researchers detected its DNA in the animal skins used to make parchment, according to the university. The York Gospels were written in Canterbury in the late 900s by Anglo-Saxon scribes and were later brought to York Minster — where they've been housed for centuries. Unexpectedly, researchers found traces of sheeppox virus on parchment made from calfskin and goatskin, suggesting either cross-species infections or contamination during the parchment-making process. Comparing the manuscripts with DNA recovered from Bronze Age sheep teeth, researchers found that sheeppox has plagued livestock for over 3,700 years. LOST SERMONS FROM ONE OF CHRISTIANITY'S GREATEST SAINTS DISCOVERED AFTER 1,600 YEARS In a statement, UCD described the York Gospels as a "biological time capsule" that preserved evidence of the virus for centuries. "The research reveals that sheeppox has threatened livestock for more than 3,700 years," the university said. "Unlike other skeletal material, teeth can preserve genetic evidence of infection over thousands of years, providing a valuable record of past outbreaks." Sheeppox can spread rapidly through flocks and can be deadly, particularly for young animals — making outbreaks a potentially serious threat to livestock-dependent communities. "A highly contagious disease, sheeppox spreads rapidly and can affect large portions of a flock in a short time," UCD said. EXPERTS STUNNED AFTER UNCOVERING HOMER'S 'ILIAD' ON EGYPTIAN MUMMY IN UNPRECEDENTED FIND "The disease is particularly dangerous because it can cause very high mortality rates, especially in young animals, and dramatically reduce productivity by damaging wool, meat and milk yields." Louis L'Hôte, a Ph.D. candidate at UCD who was the lead author of the study, told university officials that the discovery shows parchment can preserve traces of animal pathogen DNA for centuries. "It is possible that archives and libraries around the world also contain the genetic traces of disease outbreaks in animals in the past," said L'Hôte. "These genomes help us understand how these pathogens evolved and how they affected past societies — such as sheeppox virus, which we show has been affecting Eurasian sheep herds for at least three-and-a-half millennia." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER L'Hôte added that the pathogen remains a threat today — and that studying its ancient DNA could help researchers better understand how to eradicate it. "We find that unlike the smallpox virus, the sheeppox virus genome was very stable over the last few millennia." "People around the world are still fighting against this pathogen — there is currently an outbreak of sheeppox in Greece, causing much economic damage," he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "We find that unlike the smallpox virus, the sheeppox virus genome was very stable over the last few millennia," he added. "This might mean that genetic changes before this point were very important to how the sheeppox virus evolved to infect its host, which may help us fight the pathogen in the future," he added. Fox News Digital reached out to L'Hôte for further comment and insight. Earlier this year, scientists discovered smallpox DNA in centuries-old Chilean mummies — providing the first evidence of the disease in that part of South America during the early colonial period. articles.title: Vape store clerks near Ole Miss campus jailed, facing drug charges
articles.summary: Bank records linked two University of Mississippi students to Oxford vape shop purchases before their deaths, according to a newly unsealed DEA affidavit.
articles.body: Two Oxford, Mississippi vape store clerks are facing federal drug charges after investigators say they traced purchases made by two University of Mississippi students before their deaths, according to court documents detailing. Yahya Mohamed Mosleh and Islam Yahya Mosleh are each charged with possession with intent to distribute a controlled substance, the documents show. According to a DEA affidavit, bank records linked Aidan Hamilton to purchases at Puffs Vape Tobacco & Beer and Robert Strang to Express Mart #7 before investigators recovered similar suspected kratom products at both death scenes. Authorities also describe undercover purchases and the seizure of more than 500 suspected kratom-related products from the Oxford vape shop. The affidavit dated Sept. 25 says investigators were still awaiting toxicology results from the medical examiner at the time. OLE MISS STUDENTS DIED NEAR DRUG LISTING NEWLY ILLEGAL INGREDIENT, EX-PROSECUTOR SAYS SELLING IT IS 'UNLAWFUL' The charges come as officials await the toxicology results from the deaths of Ole Miss students Aidan Hamilton, 18, and Robert Strang, 20. Both students were found dead with similar packages of synthetic kratom found to be in their possession, court documents say. The Mosleh's aren't accused in either deaths. READ THE COURT COMPLAINT: Packaging on the kratom items found near both men were labeled "Smax, Pseudo-DHM" tablets, which is a "Kratom like substance at gas stations or tobacco shops" that people buy for the "narcotic like effect," according to the court documents. SEND US A TIP In September, Hamilton made multiple purchases at Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford, where employees Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, 51, and Islam Mohamed, 18, were arrested Friday on a state-level charge of possession of a controlled substance with intent to distribute, according to officials. Court documents did not establish that the kratom discovered near Hamilton at the time of his death originated from that store. One of those purchases occurred the day before Hamilton was found dead. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X According to court records, a confidential law enforcement informant visited Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store and inquired whether the store carried "7 O Kratom based pills." A store clerk responded "yes," then opened a drawer beneath the register and produced a package of kratom. Mosleh allegedly told the informant to "be quiet" about the pills and to be careful taking them because "people were dying from them." articles.title: 18 warships, wider global reach: Indian Navy eyes biggest-ever fleet expansion
articles.summary: 2026 is shaping up to be a landmark year for the Indian Navy, with plans to induct or commission as many as 18 warships, the largest single-year addition
articles.body: 2026 is shaping up to be a landmark year for the Indian Navy, with plans to induct or commission as many as 18 warships, the largest single-year addition to the fleet in the Navy's history.The scale of the expansion was highlighted at the Navy's biannual Commanders' Conference, held at Nausena Bhawan in New Delhi. The developments were described as a reflection of the growing maturity of India's domestic naval shipbuilding ecosystem.At the conference, India's position in the Indian Ocean Region was also highlighted, with the country increasingly seen as a first responder and preferred security partner. Its strategic responsibilities are expanding amid a more complex maritime environment marked by congestion, deception and so-called grey-zone activities. The Navy emphasised the need to strengthen monitoring and response mechanisms, including a significant upgrade of India's maritime surveillance architecture to keep pace with the growing volume and complexity of maritime traffic.The Navy's expanding reach beyond its traditional area of operations was another key focus. Indian warships are currently deployed in the South China Sea, the Mediterranean and the Atlantic Ocean, underscoring the force's blue-water capability and growing role in providing strategic depth and power projection. This expanding maritime footprint was linked to the broader vision of Viksit Bharat 2047, with the Navy's role extending beyond protecting India's maritime boundaries to safeguarding economic interests and contributing to regional stability.Defence minister Rajnath Singh particularly praised the Navy's role during the recent crisis in West Asia, highlighting its efforts to ensure the safe passage of Indian-flagged merchant vessels, including LPG tankers, through the Strait of Hormuz under Operation Urja Suraksha.The security of these sea lanes has direct implications for India's economic and energy security. India imports roughly 85-90% of its crude oil and around half of its natural gas by sea, making the uninterrupted movement of energy supplies through key maritime chokepoints critical to the country's economy.Minister of State for Electronics and IT Jitin Prasada, who addressed the Naval Commanders, also lauded the Navy's role in safeguarding India's energy security. He highlighted the government's parallel push to strengthen India's sovereignty in semiconductor and chip production and build a more resilient technology ecosystem.Prasada was briefed on the Navy's efforts towards innovation, indigenisation and technology absorption. He also highlighted the growing importance of artificial intelligence, quantum technologies and other emerging technologies for both the wider technology ecosystem and the armed forces.Pointing to critical choke points in defence trade and their links with emerging technologies, Prasada reiterated the government's commitment to ensuring the rapid and effective absorption of new technologies as part of a tech-enabled and self-reliant defence ecosystem.The Navy's growing indigenous capability was another major theme at the conference. Recently commissioned warships were noted to carry more than 75% indigenous content, with India's naval shipbuilding ecosystem now being described as capable of meeting global benchmarks. The focus, however, is increasingly shifting from meeting domestic requirements to developing the capacity to export warships to friendly nations.The conference also reviewed the Navy's progress on women's empowerment under its 'all ranks, all roles' approach. Women officers are now serving on frontline warships and aircraft and participating in major expeditions, including the Navika Sagar Parikrama voyage.India's recent assumption of command of Combined Task Force-154 under the Combined Maritime Forces was also highlighted as an important contribution to regional cooperative security. The Navy's Operation Southern Readiness in Kochi brought together 276 personnel from 27 countries, while the deployment of INS Sudarshini for Lokayan-26 strengthened India's maritime diplomacy and engagement with the Indian diaspora across the US, Atlantic and Mediterranean regions.The three-day Commanders' Conference, held from September 29 to October 1, brought together the Navy's top leadership to review operational preparedness, maritime security and future capability development.

articles.title: Former Arizona fraternity leader sentenced to jail time after pledge dies in off-campus hazing
articles.summary: Carter Eslick, former Northern Arizona University fraternity leader, pleaded guilty to felony hazing in the alcohol poisoning death of a pledge.
articles.body: A former fraternity leader at Northern Arizona University was sentenced to two months in jail on Wednesday for his role in a hazing incident that led to the death of a student. Carter Eslick, 20, pleaded guilty to a felony hazing charge in Coconino County Superior Court for the Jan. 31 death of Colin Daniel Martinez. Eslick served as the Delta Tau Delta pledge master at the time of the incident. Martinez died at a Delta Tau Delta off-campus house due to alcohol poisoning, with an autopsy finding a blood-alcohol content of 0.45% shortly after his death. LSU FRAT PLEDGES ALLEGEDLY WATERBOARDED, FORCED TO CHUG MILK IN HAZING RITUALS: REPORT During the hazing, Martinez was among a group of four pledges who drank two bottles of vodka to ensure that they vomited, according to NBC News. Hazing witnesses said they attempted to monitor the sleeping Martinez for signs of alcohol poisoning, adjusting his sleeping position multiple times. Eslick told the court, where Martinez's parents were present, that he takes "full responsibility for the hand I played in that ritual." The sentencing comes amid headlines regarding the mysterious deaths of two students at Ole Miss — one of whom was in a fraternity — and an alleged frat cocaine distribution ring at Penn State. PENN STATE FRATERNITY COCAINE DEALS GREW TO KILO LOADS AS PLEDGES HELPED PACKAGE DRUGS, WITNESSES TESTIFY One of the Ole Miss students who was found dead this past week, Robert Strang, was a Phi Delta Theta fraternity brother. He was found at an off-campus home. Authorities found packages of kratom, a commercially available drug that has been derided as "gas station heroin," at the sites of both deaths. However, its role in either death was not immediately clear. Phi Delta Theta has not been accused of any wrongdoing. OLE MISS STUDENTS' TOXICOLOGY REPORTS WILL BE DONE 'IN DUE COURSE,' FAMILIES TO BE NOTIFIED FIRST: OFFICIALS "The loss of two young lives is a profound tragedy," the fraternity said in a statement. "Phi Delta Theta joins the University of Mississippi and the broader Ole Miss community in mourning Robert and Aidan Hamilton and extending our deepest sympathies to their families, friends, chapter brothers, classmates, and all those who knew and loved them." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "These losses reinforce the importance of a collective commitment to health, safety, and well-being on college campuses today. We encourage the Phi Delta Theta community to keep the Strang family, the Mississippi Alpha Chapter, and everyone affected by these tragic losses in their thoughts," the statement continued.

articles.title: Zimbabwe businessman Wicknell Chivayo killed in helicopter crash
articles.summary: The high-profile businessman known for his political connections was one of six people killed in the crash.
articles.body:
Wicknell Chivayo, one of Zimbabwe’s best-known businessmen, has died along with his wife, Lucy Muteke, and four others after a private helicopter crashed in a rural area east of the capital, Harare.

State broadcaster ZBC reported that the group of six had set off on Wednesday from Gandami, a rural area in Chikomba district where Chivayo grew up and where he and his wife were building a home.

The helicopter crashed about 40 minutes after takeoff at Kudenga Farm near Marondera, a town about 70km (45 miles) southeast of Harare. Government spokesperson Nick Mangwana said on X that there were “no survivors”.

Herbert Chivayo, a spokesperson for the family, confirmed the deaths to ZBC.

Forensic experts and investigators were sent to the site on Thursday morning, according to Zimbabwean newspaper The Herald. Transport and Infrastructural Development Minister Felix Mhona was among the senior officials expected to visit.

George Mashababe, director-general of the Civil Aviation Authority of Zimbabwe, said early indications were that the helicopter’s tail hit the ground first. He told The Herald the impact caused fuel to spill, and that the resulting fire followed the fuel across the ground.

Mashababe said the inquiry was ongoing and that a full statement would be issued later.

Chivayo, who was in his 40s, was the founder of Intratrek Zimbabwe, a company involved in major energy projects, including the long-delayed 100-megawatt Gwanda solar project.

His ambitions extended beyond Zimbabwe’s borders. In June, King Mswati III granted him Eswatini citizenship and a diplomatic passport, after which Chivayo announced plans for a 300MW solar project in the Southern African kingdom.

He was equally known for his public persona. Styling himself “Sir Wicknell”, he chronicled his lavish lifestyle on social media, where posts about luxury purchases and gifts to friends drew both admiration and criticism. A 2025 report in the Zimbabwean newspaper The Standard said he had spent about $9.3m on vehicles and other gifts for his associates.

He also cultivated close ties with politicians and influential figures across Africa.

Kenyan President William Ruto paid tribute to Chivayo as “a dear friend whose warmth touched many people”. Writing on X, he said he would remember Chivayo for his friendship, energy and belief in what the African continent could achieve. Ruto also offered his condolences to Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa and the people of the country.

articles.title: New US visa rule from October 1: Expanded social media screening for I, TN and TD visa applicants

articles.body: Starting on October 1, 2026, the US Department of State will check the social media accounts of I-1, TN, and TD visa applicants. These visa applicants will have to make all their social media profiles public for review by visa officials. Social media vetting is already in place for H-1B/H4, F-1/F-2, J-1/J-2, H-3, K, R, Q, T/U/S visa applicants. articles.title: Captain Smit Machchhar: Friend on Indian pilot hailed as a hero
articles.summary: Capt Smit Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard the Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv.
articles.body:
When Captain Dharav Gosalia first heard what had happened to his old friend Smit Machchhar, he had one immediate reaction.

The two men have known each other since they were about 20, when they were neighbours in Ghatkopar, a Mumbai suburb, and began their flying training in New Zealand.

Machchhar was Gosalia's senior. They later spent six years as colleagues at SpiceJet, flying Boeing 737s, before their careers took them in different directions. Machchhar moved to Dubai and joined Flydubai in 2022. Gosalia went on to fly Boeing 777s for Air India.

"We have been in touch with messages," Gosalia says. "If there are some routes we have to fly, we discuss destinations and family on WhatsApp and phone."

Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?

Sometimes their paths crossed in the air, too. In 2024, Gosalia was flying to London through Dubai airspace when he recognised Machchhar's voice on the radio. Machchhar was flying to Mumbai.

On Wednesday, Machchhar was captain of a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when another pilot attacked and stabbed him in the cockpit. The Boeing 737 Max was diverted to Tabuk in north-western Saudi Arabia, where Machchhar was taken to hospital.

He remains in a stable condition, according to the Indian embassy in Riyadh.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has called Machchhar a "true hero", saying he saved the lives of 174 people and prevented a "catastrophic mid-air disaster".

For Gosalia, however, the man at the centre of the extraordinary incident is still "Smit Mac" – the nickname used by his friends and colleagues.

"He was a fun guy, gentleman – very brilliant person," he says. "Outgoing person, jovial. Very jovial."

They would meet during layovers in places such as Milan and Bangkok, and play tennis-ball cricket when they were back in Mumbai. Machchhar also helped younger pilots, teaching new recruits and passing on what he had learnt.

"He was a very disciplined flier," Gosalia says.

That discipline was reinforced by years of training, including from former Indian Air Force pilots who moved into commercial aviation.

"That training gives you more focus, more discipline, and more focus on motor skills," Gosalia says.

One part of that training, he says, is known among pilots as "chair flying": rehearsing an emergency procedure while sitting in a chair, mentally running through the sequence and moving your hands to where the relevant switches and controls would be in the cockpit.

The idea is to make those movements instinctive when something goes wrong and there is little time to think.

Machchhar had plenty of experience to draw on. He had more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile.

Gosalia says the exact sequence of Wednesday's confrontation will become clearer from the aircraft's flight data and cockpit recordings. But whatever happened inside the cockpit, he says, Machchhar had to make decisions under an extraordinary kind of pressure.

"What happened to him, what he did – he was the commander on the flight," Gosalia says.

For a pilot, there are procedures for an engine failure, a fire or a loss of cabin pressure. There is no conventional checklist for another person trying to overpower you in the cockpit.

And that, Gosalia says, is where courage matters.

"How much courage plays a role? A lot," he says. "This was a threat to life."

Then comes the thought that perhaps best explains why the incident has affected him so deeply.

"Smit has taught us courage. Now we will do the same thing if something like this happens."

articles.title: Botswana at 60 challenges the story of postcolonial African failure
articles.summary: Botswana showed that resource wealth need not condemn a country to corruption and underdevelopment.
articles.body:
This week, Botswana is marking 60 years of independence from Britain with Diamond Jubilee celebrations across the country. The anniversary underscores the scale of the country’s transformation. In 1966, the former Bechuanaland Protectorate was among the world’s poorest countries, with barely 12 kilometres of paved road, just 22 university graduates and about 100 secondary-school graduates.

Six decades later, Botswana is an upper-middle-income country with one of postcolonial Africa’s most striking development records. Between 1965 and 1980, Botswana’s economy grew by an average of 13.9 percent a year. By 2025, gross domestic product (GDP) per capita had reached about $7,800, higher than South Africa’s roughly $6,600, a striking reversal given South Africa’s position as one of the continent’s largest and most diversified economies. But the significance of Botswana’s growth lies not only in its scale, but in what the country did with it.

In 1994, it became the first country ever to graduate from the United Nations’ least-developed country category. The World Bank now classifies Botswana as an upper-middle-income economy, and the change is visible across the country. By 2024, its road network stretched almost 35,000 kilometres, 80.2 percent of the population had access to electricity and, according to the 2022 census, 66.5 percent of Batswana lived in urban areas, compared with just 9.1 percent in 1971.

Public investment also dramatically expanded access to education. By 2022, Botswana had 192,151 secondary-school pupils, while by 2024 some 60,287 students were enrolled in tertiary institutions. A country that entered independence with only 22 university graduates now educates tens of thousands of students at tertiary level.

The gains extended beyond education. Botswana’s national poverty rate fell from 30.6 percent in 2002/03 to an estimated 14.5 percent by 2022. Public healthcare expanded alongside this transformation. Today, 85 percent of Batswana live within five kilometres of a health facility and almost all births occur in health facilities.

Botswana’s response to HIV is more remarkable still. In 2002, Botswana launched Africa’s first national free comprehensive HIV treatment programme. Twenty-three years later, the World Health Organization recognised it as the first high-HIV-burden country in the world to achieve Gold Tier status on the path towards eliminating mother-to-child transmission. Ninety-eight percent of pregnant women living with HIV receive treatment, transmission to children has fallen to about 1.2 percent and life expectancy now stands at 69 years.

Political stability has also endured through democratic change. In 2024, after 58 years of Botswana Democratic Party rule, voters elected the opposition Umbrella for Democratic Change (UDC) and the outgoing government relinquished office peacefully.

Botswana’s achievements are increasingly visible beyond politics and economics, too. Letsile Tebogo won the country’s first Olympic gold medal in Paris in 2024. A year later, Collen Kebinatshipi became world 400m champion. In May 2026, Botswana hosted the World Athletics Relays in Gaborone, a first for Africa, and ended the competition by winning the men’s 4x400m title before its home crowd.

Behind much of Botswana’s economic and social progress lies the way it has managed its diamond wealth.

Today, Botswana owns 50 percent of Debswana, the diamond-mining joint venture it shares with De Beers, while the Pula Fund, its sovereign wealth fund, preserves part of the country’s wealth for future generations and helps cushion the economy against mineral-related macroeconomic shocks. Foreign reserves equivalent to 7.5 months of imports provide an additional layer of financial protection. The state continues to use mineral revenues to finance public services, infrastructure and economic development rather than treating diamonds simply as an export windfall.

Yet for all that Botswana has achieved, it remains vulnerable to the commodity that financed much of this progress. Diamonds have accounted for almost 90 percent of goods exports over the past decade and still generate about a third of national revenue and three-quarters of foreign-exchange earnings.

Natural diamonds have faced softer luxury demand and growing competition from laboratory-grown stones that sell for a fraction of the price. As global demand weakened, Botswana felt the consequences immediately. The economy contracted by 2.8 percent in 2024 and another 0.7 percent in 2025.

The downturn deepens Botswana’s already serious employment challenge. Its latest household survey puts unemployment at 21 percent, rising to 28.9 percent among people aged 15 to 35.

Botswana largely avoided the resource curse, yet it never overcame its heavy reliance on diamonds. The challenge at 60 is no longer how to turn diamonds into development, but how to create prosperity that can survive without them.

That requires looking beyond diamonds. Botswana’s 2025 agreement with De Beers gives the state-owned Okavango Diamond Company 30 percent of Debswana production, rising to 40 percent after 2030 and potentially 50 percent thereafter. It also provides for jewellery manufacturing, diamond grading and vocational training. Botswana should capture as much value as possible from every stone it mines. But processing, polishing and marketing diamonds will not end its dependence on diamonds.

Botswana now needs a broader, more resilient economy, and some of the foundations are already in place. In 2024, 68.9 percent of households had internet access, up from 40.6 percent a decade earlier. That connectivity has yet to translate into many jobs: information and communications technology accounted for only 2 percent of employment in 2025. Botswana must invest in the skills needed to turn connectivity into software, fintech, digital services and technology businesses that employ Batswana and sell beyond its borders.

Tourism is another existing strength, already providing about 50,500 jobs, or 6.7 percent of total employment, and accounting for more than 60 percent of services exports. A conservation model that places roughly 40 percent of the country’s land under protected status gives Botswana an asset it can build on.

Economic diversification will require abundant power. A 500MW solar plant with 500MWh of battery storage is being built at Maun. Cheap, reliable renewable energy could support manufacturing, data centres and new industries rather than simply light homes.

Botswana must also help more businesses compete regionally and globally. More than 95 percent of private-sector sales remain domestic and only 9 percent of surveyed firms export at all. More Batswana need access to finance and training so they can start, own and expand businesses and benefit from the next economy.

The institutions that turned diamonds into roads, schools and healthcare must now use six decades of accumulated skills, infrastructure and capital to create a new economy built on technology, energy, manufacturing and exports.

Botswana matters beyond its borders because its record contrasts sharply with other resource-rich African states. According to the World Bank’s latest available data, copper dominates Zambia’s exports, while 71.7 percent of Zambians live on less than $3 a day. The Democratic Republic of the Congo is rich in copper and cobalt, but 85.3 percent of its people remain below the same threshold. In oil-rich Nigeria, Africa’s largest petroleum producer, 41.8 percent of the population lives on less than $3 a day.

Botswana demonstrates that a decisive question is not whether a country has mineral wealth, but who controls it, how its revenues are protected and whether the state converts them into better housing, stronger infrastructure, reliable public services and greater economic security.

That lesson is especially important as African countries seek greater control over critical minerals. Mineral wealth does not inevitably produce corruption, conflict or poverty. Success must ultimately be measured by whether those resources foster more productive economies, widen opportunity and materially improve people’s lives.

That is the larger meaning of Botswana at 60: in the right hands, postcolonial power can serve the many rather than the few.

There is an old Setswana saying: “Moenyane o pele lebone la waabo” — the one who goes ahead becomes a light for those who come after.

articles.title: Family awaits word on mother-daughter missing in Nepal floods
articles.summary: Family in Odisha awaits updates from Nepal authorities after a 25-year-old woman and her 2-year-old daughter went missing in Aug 26 flash floods; DNA samples collected.
articles.body: Rourkela: More than a month after a 25-year-old Odisha woman and her two-year-old daughter went missing in flash floods in Nepal on Aug 26, their family is still awaiting information from Nepal authorities, despite DNA samples being collected for identification. Kamma Venkatesh (22), of Kullunda Jamtikra village under Atabira block in Bargarh district and the younger brother of missing woman Gunnam Sai Bindu, travelled to Kathmandu last month to provide a DNA sample sought by officials.Venkatesh said Bindu had video-called him at around 8.28am on Aug 26 and spoken for nearly six minutes, even showing him her daughter, Harixa. A few minutes later, the flash floods struck. The family learnt of their disappearance the following day from Bindu’s husband, Gunnam Jaykrishna (38). Venkatesh’s sample was collected in Kathmandu on Sept 4 for comparison with unidentified remains recovered after the disaster. “Nearly a month has passed, but we have received no update from the Nepal govt. My mother is heartbroken,” he said.Jaykrishna survived the floods while working at the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in Rasuwa district. He was on higher ground when the floods hit, but Bindu and Harixa, who were at home in a nearby village, remain untraceable. Jaykrishna was airlifted to Kathmandu on Aug 27 and stayed back to search for them with company support. His travel documents were washed away. He returned to Bargarh on Sept 5. articles.title: Newborn baby found near Bangor may have been in water for weeks
articles.summary: The body of the baby found along the north Wales shoreline was a girl, a post-mortem has revealed.
articles.body:
The body of a baby girl found along a north Wales shoreline may have been in the water for up to a few weeks, according to initial indications.

A member of the public found the body on the Menai Strait shoreline near Siliwen Road in Bangor, Gwynedd, on Sunday shortly before 17:00 BST.

In an update on Thursday, North Wales Police said a post-mortem revealed the newborn baby was a girl.

The force are continuing the search for the mother and urged her to make contact with police.

Further tests to find more about the baby are under way, North Wales Police said.

"We understand that the mother may be fearful of coming forward but we urge her to make contact with us," Supt Llinos Davies said, adding that she wanted to reassure her that her welfare and safety was their "utmost concern".

"Anyone with concerns about a girl or a woman you think may have been pregnant or whose behaviour has been unusual or out of character over the past few months including withdrawing from friends, family or social ties, please contact us," Davies said.

She said all names received would be treated with the utmost discretion and can be eliminated as the mother without delay.

"I understand that this is a terribly sad incident for the community and I am grateful for the overwhelming support and assistance that we have received so far," Davies said.

Fiona Giraud, director of midwifery and women's services for Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board, said her priority remained with the mother.

Addressing her, she said: "Our immediate concern remains to be your health, safety and wellbeing.

"You may feel you have nowhere to turn, or that you cannot speak to anyone about what has happened. Please do not feel that you have to face this alone," she said.

"We don't yet know all the circumstances surrounding your baby's death, but what is important right now is that we find you, make sure you are safe and ensure you receive any medical attention and support you may need.

"I am asking you personally, please take the first step and contact us. There are people to help you," Giraud said.
